articles.excerpt: On October 21, 2026, Anthropic opened a research preview of Claude Duet, an app where Claude works as a proactive agent: it watches your connected accounts, prepares work while you are away, and messa…
articles.body: On October 21, 2026, Anthropic opened a research preview of Claude Duet, an app where Claude works as a proactive agent: it watches your connected accounts, prepares work while you are away, and messages you when something needs you. The interesting part is not that Claude can now start the conversation. It is how Anthropic moved the most important controls outside the model, and what still depends on a human tapping "approve." Here is how Duet works, what its safety design gets right, where the real risks are, and how I would use it today. Research and product status checked November 14, 2026. Twelve Approvals Before Lunch Imagine it is Monday, 7:40 a.m. Before you open your laptop, a message is waiting on your phone. Claude has already read your inbox and calendar.
articles.author: Suraj Khaitan

articles.title: The Invisible Brush: Generative Art and the Algorithms That Paint
articles.excerpt: A long-form exploration of Procedural Content Generation as a creative engine — with Clojure and Quil. There is a particular kind of wonder that comes from watching something grow on a screen that you…
articles.body: A long-form exploration of Procedural Content Generation as a creative engine — with Clojure and Quil. There is a particular kind of wonder that comes from watching something grow on a screen that you did not draw. A tree that branches unpredictably. A coastline that stretches further than any hand could trace. A galaxy of stars no astronomer catalogued. You wrote the rules, but the world surprised you anyway. This is the promise of Procedural Content Generation — and it sits quietly at the heart of generative art. This post is for developers who can read code but have never thought of algorithms as paintbrushes.
articles.author: Ganesh Rajendran

articles.title: Event ID 4673 flood: why the Security log is full and the PC is slow
articles.excerpt: Originally published at coinetic.io. Event 4673 is Windows saying "A privileged service was called". A few a day are normal. Dozens per second, from chrome.exe, msedgewebview2.exe or Code.exe, make th…
articles.body: Originally published at coinetic.io . Event 4673 is Windows saying "A privileged service was called" . A few a day are normal. Dozens per second, from chrome.exe , msedgewebview2.exe or Code.exe , make the Windows Event Log service eat whole processor cores – and the log falls minutes or hours behind. In short What it is: a program asked for a special Windows right (a privilege ), and an audit policy logs it. Typical flood: Audit Failure entries for SeProfileSingleProcessPrivilege from Chromium-based programs: Chrome, Edge, Edge WebView (used by Teams, Outlook, widgets) and VS Code. They ask for memory figures, Windows refuses, they ask again. The cause: almost always a Group Policy with Audit privilege use = Success, Failure . The fix: in that policy, untick Failure and keep Success .
articles.author: Coinetic AI Security

articles.title: I deleted my extensions.gnome.org account. My extensions stayed online.
articles.excerpt: In December 2025 I deleted my account on extensions.gnome.org, the official store for GNOME Shell extensions. I expected my three extensions to go with it. They didn't. ClipFlow Pro, Comfort Control (…
articles.body: In December 2025 I deleted my account on extensions.gnome.org, the official store for GNOME Shell extensions. I expected my three extensions to go with it. They didn't. ClipFlow Pro , Comfort Control (EaseHub) and Numeric Date And Clock are still listed there, under a placeholder account called "MaintainerWanted", with old builds I no longer control, test or support. Nothing on the deletion page warned me this would happen, and with the account gone I have no way to switch them off myself. This post is the full timeline, where it stands today, and a warning for other extension authors. The timeline 18 October 2026. I asked GNOME to remove the three listings, on the extensions.gnome.org issue tracker (on GNOME's own GitLab) and by email to the GNOME Foundation. 3–10 November.
articles.author: Nick Otmazgin

articles.body: Why this lesson exists When you run csperf run you get a JSON file that contains timing, machine metadata, and a reference to the generated LLVM IR. Many developers delete the .ll file after the run, thinking it’s just a temporary artifact. In reality, the IR is the explanation behind the numbers. Without it you lose the ability to trace why a particular optimization changed the timing. Recap — where we are in the series Ep 1 — Why a Single ./a.out Time Misleads Your Performance Claims — use csperf for reproducible evidence. Ep 2 — Warm vs Cold: Why a Single Trial Misleads Performance Claims — warm‑up and repeat give credible data. articles.title: Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents: what you run, what still leaves your network
articles.excerpt: Anthropic opened a private beta of self-hosted Claude Managed Agents on Nov 12. Access is by request through your Anthropic account team. Before this, you could self-host the sandbox where an agent's…
articles.body: Anthropic opened a private beta of self-hosted Claude Managed Agents on Nov 12. Access is by request through your Anthropic account team. Before this, you could self-host the sandbox where an agent's code runs, but Anthropic ran the rest, including credentials and the record of what each agent did. Now the whole service can sit in your cloud or on-prem. What you operate: the Managed Agents server its PostgreSQL database (session history lives here) the workers where agents run shell and file tools You build agents with the same core APIs as the hosted service. What still leaves your network is Claude itself. Model requests go where you point them: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or your own gateway. Prompts out, completions back.

articles.body: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 sees Sauron begin to recruit the nine lieutenants that will one day become the Nazgûl, or Ringraiths. While details in J.R.R. articles.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
articles.excerpt: The red planet Mars will shine a little over 1 degree from Jupiter on the night of Nov. 15-16.
articles.body: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth .

articles.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
articles.excerpt: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
articles.body: Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow. If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power , you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch. During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants.

articles.title: 20 Years Ago, the Best Sci-Fi Show of the Century Delivered the Most Epic Space Battle in TV History
articles.excerpt: Twenty years ago, Battlestar Galactica topped the Adama Maneuver by transforming the Pegasus into an enormous battering ram.
articles.body: Two decades later, this spectacle from Battlestar Galactica season 3’s “Exodus, Part 2” remains unforgettable sci-fi TV. It’s dazzling and horrifying, and still one of the coolest things ever broadcast on science-fiction television. From a tactical standpoint, the “Adama Maneuver” is absolutely bonkers and one of the riskiest spaceship tactics, perhaps ever (sorry, Vice-Admiral Holdo). What if the ship had gotten torn apart from ripping through the atmosphere? What if the FTL drive malfunctioned or didn’t activate in time? Somehow, it’s also not even the most visually impressive sequence in the episode.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX's Starship megarocket reached orbit today (Nov. 13) during its 15th test flight, but the company scrapped a plan to catch the vehicle's massive booster back at the launch site.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
articles.excerpt: 60 years ago, the Leonid meteor shower unleashed one of the most spectacular meteor storms in recorded history. As the 2026 peak approaches, here's what skywatchers can expect.
articles.body: This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed.

articles.title: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
articles.excerpt: How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century
articles.body: In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication. But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

articles.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
articles.excerpt: The California Science Center's brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center —the home of NASA's space shuttle Endeavour —officially opened to the public today (Nov. 13).
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
